utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner and Daryl Mundis, assisted by Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President -- good day, Mr. President, good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel, and Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and our legal assistant, Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 20th of April, I would like to greet everyone present, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, Mr. Bourgon who is constantly in this courtroom. I greet the accused, General Hadzihasanovic and Brigadier Kubura. Naturally, I wouldn't want to forget to mention everyone else in or around the courtroom. We'll be hearing two witnesses today. I'd like to inform the Defence that a hearing is scheduled for tomorrow afternoon. As this courtroom will be available in the morning, would it be possible for the Defence to appear in the morning rather than the afternoon if we have to have a hearing tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as Mr. Kubura's Defence is concerned, working in the morning is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that isn't a problem for us either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution is always ready at the Trial Chamber's convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could you please check to see whether the courtroom is in fact available in the morning. Before the witness comes into the courtroom, are there any issues that either of the parties would like to raise? Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Very briefly, I informed the Chamber's legal officer and the counsel for both accused prior to court today that we are in the final stages of finalising our application to re-open the Prosecution case. It is clear to us that we will not be able to condense our pleadings into the ten-page limit as prescribed by the practice direction, and we would respect request the Chamber's leave to file a motion of no longer than 20 pages. I anticipate it being actually closer to 15 to 18 pages, but for the sake of caution I would respectfully ask for 20 pages, and as the Trial Chamber is aware, there will be a number of annexes, but of course annexes are specifically excluded from the page limits by the relevant practice direction. I am hopeful that we can get that filed tomorrow, but alternatively it might be Friday or perhaps even as late as Monday. We are awaiting a few translations of some of the annexes, but we do anticipate it will be up to but certainly no longer than 20 pages, if the Trial Chamber will so permit us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will grant your request. You will be granted 20 pages, the possibility of filing 20 pages. There are no other issues to be raised. Mr. Registrar, I'll give you the floor now because we have to deal with the numbers. We have to clarify something to do with the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The day before yesterday we admitted two Defence exhibits for General Hadzihasanovic, 2020 [as interpreted] was the number. It was said to be under seal; that was a mistake. DH2163 had an English version DH2163/E. [In English] DH2163 and DH2163/E which is admitted under seal and confidential. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this information. Mr. Usher, could you call the first witness into the courtroom, please. How much time does Defence counsel think they will need for the first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll need no more than approximately 45 minutes for examination-in-chief. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, and I can add that there are no maps or documents to be shown to this first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a question for General Hadzihasanovic's Defence counsel. The Judges examined the issue yesterday. As far as the questions that you put to witnesses after the questions put to witnesses by Mr. Kubura's Defence counsel is concerned, we would like to know whether General Hadzihasanovic's Defence is an independent team, a team independent of Mr. Kubura's Defence team. Because up until now our impression was that you were in a certain sense acting together. Or are you a unified team? The consequences would not be same. If you're an independent Defence team, you have the right to cross-examine and to put leading questions to witnesses. But if you are to be considered as a single team, as a unified team, in such a case you don't have the right to put leading questions to the witness. All you can do is conduct your examination-in-chief and put neutral questions to witnesses. That is the situation, and depending on the way you consider yourselves, you will be allowed to examine in one way or another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, from the very beginning of this case on a number of occasions we have said that the Defence team for General Hadzihasanovic is independent of Brigadier Kubura's Defence team; both teams acting independently. However, it's true that in exceptional situations, there are certain common elements shared by the Defence teams. And we informed the Trial Chamber of the fact on a number of occasions. We have filed joint motions, and that was mentioned in the motions concerned. And we treated our expert witnesses as common expert witnesses because they testified about issues that concerned the professional knowledge they had, the expert knowledge they had. It's only in those three occasions -- on those three occasions that we had witnesses that were common to both teams. So, in conclusion, General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team is acting independently, which is also the case for Brigadier Kubura's Defence team. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As a conclusion drawn by the Judges the other day, and that is that if you are an independent team the party to ask the last questions after the Judges' questions is the party that has called the witness. Do we agree on that? As far as this rather complex issue is concerned, what would the Prosecution like to say? Any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we will proceed in the light of what you have just said. As you are an independent Defence team, you have the right to cross-examine, you can ask questions after the Judges' questions. Brigadier Kubura's Defence team has no objections, no comments to make? Very well. We are in agreement. In that case, we will now call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that the equipment is functioning correctly. Can you -- are you receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying? If so, please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So before you take the solemn declaration, could you please tell me your first and last names, your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Elvedin Omic. I was born on the 29th of December, 1972, in Zenica, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, are you currently employed? Do you hold a position of any kind? And if so, what kind of position do you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am an officer in the Federation army, in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I currently work for MONUC which is a UN mission in Congo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have said you are an officer. What is your rank? A captain? A general? What is your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you have a post of any kind? If you were in the military, which unit were you in and what rank did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 I was a soldier. In June 1992 I joined the Bosnia and Herzegovina Territorial Defence, and in 1993, in March, I joined the 7th Muslim Brigade, again in the capacity of a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, have you already testified before a national or international court with regard to the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified before; this is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down, Major. Before I give the floor to the Defence team for their examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that we will be following here. First you will have to answer the questions put to you by Brigadier Kubura's Defence team. They expect that their examination-in-chief will last about 45 minutes. After that stage, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will conduct what we call the cross-examination, and they will probably take the same amount of time, three-quarters of an hour. Then the Defence team, to your left -- but I forgot to mention that General Hadzihasanovic's Defence may also put questions to you if they wish to do so. But once the Prosecution has completed its cross-examination, Defence counsel may re-examine you. The three Judges sitting before you may at any point in time put questions to you, but we prefer to wait for the end of the questions because quite frequently the matters that interest us have been dealt with -- will have been dealt with and there is no reason for us to intervene. We might intervene in order to obtain clarifications from you or because we believe that there are some gaps in your testimony. And it would be in the interest of justice to put some questions to you. As you are a member of the military, we might ask you questions that are purely technical and military questions. After this stage, or during your testimony, the parties may show you documents, military documents, or documents from the 7th Brigade. I should also like to point out the following: You've just taken the solemn declaration which means that you should not give false testimony, as you are well aware, especially since you are an officer. And as a witness, you may refuse to answer a question in particular if you think that the question -- the answer could subsequently be used against you, to level charges against you. Rest assured this is a case that we have never had to deal with to date. But if such a case should arise, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question, but the Chamber grants the witness a form of immunity. This is all very technical, but it's a difficulty that we have never encountered. The procedure followed is an oral procedure, this is why you will see everything that is being said transcribed on the screen that is in front of you, and this is why your answers are so important. Try to answer the questions as fully as possible in order to assist the Judges when they have to assess all the evidence presented. If you run into difficulties of any kind, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. As we will be having a break every one and a half hour, we will probably be having a break at about 3.30 or 3.40, a 20 or 25-minute break. This is how we will be proceedings, and without wasting any more time, I will now give the floor to Defence counsel, who will conduct the examination-in-chief. I see that it is Mr. Dixon who has already got his lectern in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Dixon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Omic. You said in response to a question asked by the President that you are currently working for the UN mission, MONUC, in the Congo. Can you explain from when you have been stationed in the Congo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I've been in the Congo since November 2004, since the 25th of November, 2004, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you assigned to go there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I was selected by the General Staff; they suggested that I should go there. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina sent me to be part of the UN mission in the Congo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your role in the UN mission?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I work as a military observer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What functions do you perform as a military observer?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Currently I'm in Bukavu, the town of Bukavu, I work at the airport. I monitor local flights. Arms embargo tasks are involved, the import and export of weapons from Congo. Sometimes we carry out controls in other areas and we inform the authorities of these controls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who do you work with as part of the UN mission?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I work with my colleagues from other countries. There are currently five of us in the team. One of them is from Paraguay, there is another person in Indonesia, a third person is from Morocco, the fourth person is from Nepal, and I'm the fifth person from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before your UN mission to Congo, had you had any other international experience with the Bosnian army outside of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before I went to the Congo I was trained in various other countries, trained in peacekeeping operations. The training was in Romania, Greece, and Malaysia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to take you back now to the start of your military career. When and where did you receive your military training?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Initially I was in the JNA; I received my military training there. I went to serve in the JNA as a recruit. That was in June 1991. I remained there for three months, up until September 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you receive this training in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: In a town called Sabac, which is in the western part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave this town and can you explain to the Trial Chamber why you left?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I left the town, or rather I left the JNA and returned home in September 1991, because as a recruit in the barracks I had seen a lot of Serbian volunteers. They weren't regular troops. There were a lot of Serbian volunteers who had gathered there, and they would be sent from there to the battlefield in Croatia. After all those events, I spoke to my family members -- I spoke to my father, to be more precise, and he ordered me to return home. He told me to return home and to leave the former Yugoslavian army, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omic, where is home?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: In Zenica, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive back home?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Well, it was at the beginning of September 1991, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived back in Zenica, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: When I arrived back in Zenica, since JNA units were still present in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I couldn't sleep at home. I spent more than two months in hiding because there was the possibility of the former JNA military police coming to arrest me. And that is why during that period I spent more than two months, during which I slept in the houses of relatives of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not want to serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to remain in the JNA because at the time the JNA was engaged in the battlefield in Croatia and they were fighting the Croats, and I didn't want to be part of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come out of hiding after two months, was the time period you mentioned, and what did you do at that stage?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: After two months -- I know the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina took a decision according to which young men from Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have to go and serve in the JNA. So I went to the Secretariat of Defence in Zenica municipality. I went to report there, and I told them when I left the JNA, and I told them that I was currently in the town of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: They told me that that wasn't a problem and that I wouldn't suffer any consequences for what I had done. They said that I could go home in peace. And that was at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving then into 1992, did you at any time in 1992 continue with your military service and how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: In April 1992, after all those events, I once again went to that defence secretariat of the municipality of Zenica and asked to be mobilised and included in the Territorial Defence units. I wanted to join the Territorial Defence in defending my country, but I was told that they were unable to mobilise me at that stage because there were not enough weapons. And I was told to go home. That was in April 1992. I waited for a while. And then on a number of occasions I went to see them, but every single time they told me they had no weapons. And then in June of 1992 I finally went there again and I said that I simply would not leave unless I was mobilised, and then I was sent to a unit. That was the 1st Zenica Brigade, the 1st Battalion, and that's when I was mobilised as soldier. And at first, I did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time that you received a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: It was perhaps some 20 days after my joining that unit, when we went -- when my unit was sent to Visoko, and after those of us who stayed behind in Zenica had to replace them, to take over their shift in that area in the municipality of Visoko, the ones going on leave gave their arms to us, since we were going to replace them. And that was the first time I got any weapons from the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move ahead now to 1993. Did you join any unit of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993 and when was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the armed forces of the units within the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- well, since June 1992, but by the end of that year I was seriously ill. I had severe pneumonia, and the medical commission released me from military service, and that was in the beginning of March 1993. And when I was given that letter, I went to the secretariat once again and asked to be mobilised notwithstanding, that is to say, in spite of the fact that I had been ill, because I had recovered then. And I was again mobilised in March 1993, and I joined the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which unit of the 7th Brigade were you mobilised into?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: That was the 2nd Battalion, the 1st Company, the 1st Platoon, and the 1st Squad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any rank?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: No. At that stage I was a simple soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you based at that time, in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: We were stationed at the secondary school at Bilmiste.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In June of 1993, do you recall being engaged into a military operation and could you assist the Trial Chamber with how that happened?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: By the beginning of June we had two operations. Whilst I was in that unit, Ovnak and Kakanj, those were the two operations. How it came to that on that day in the beginning of June, I really can't remember the exact date. I think it was on the 7th or 8th of June -- the 6th or the 7th, I'm not sure, and the commander of our squad came to see us in the morning and he told us to get ready and that we were going to engage in an operation. We asked him where we were meant to go, but he answered that he was in no position to tell us at that stage, that we just had to carry out all the necessary military preparations for such an operation. On that day we carried out our preparations, and in the evening, in the early evening hours, we were taken to the bus in front of the building at Bilmiste. And a company commander came along and he told us that the operation would be at Ovnak. Thereupon, we boarded the buses. We were driven to a place called Pojske and we got there that night. We spent the night there then. And the day after, we spent the entire day at that village called Pojske. And the following night we set off and started the operation, and the following morning, early in the morning -- actually, the information [as interpretation] started at Ovnak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if there could just be a clarification for the transcript. You said the information started at Ovnak. Should that be the operation started at Ovnak. If you could just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the operation, not the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the operation at Ovnak last?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I remember that it did not take very long. The operation started in the early morning hours. Initially the HVO offered resistance for no longer than an hour, and afterwards they stopped their resistance. And I think we completed our task at some point around noon, at lunchtime, early lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the operation was completed, what orders did you receive at that point, at lunchtime on that day?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: When the operation was completed, the squad commander issued the order to gather and to follow the situation and make sure that there is no counter-attack on the part of the HVO and to take some rest. Those are the orders that we received upon completing this operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have said that the operation was in the Ovnak area. Did you stay in the Ovnak area that entire day or how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That operation was in the area of Ovnak. We stayed there all day until sunset. And at sunset, the company commander came and issued the orders to go back to the village of Pojske.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away is that approximately from the Ovnak area where the operation was?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Not far at all. I think some three to four kilometres, no more than that. It could be less, but it's certainly not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get back there from the Ovnak area?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you arrive there on that day, in Pojske this is?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I don't know at what time, but I do know that it was in the early evening hours, not late at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay the night there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We spent the night at Pojske.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the next orders that you received?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: The squad commander informed us that we would be spending the night there, and that was the orders that we received for that night. On the following day at some point at around 11.00 maybe, a bit after breakfast, the squad commander came along again and he asked us to get ready for another operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this operation to take place?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: That operation took place at Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave for Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: We left for Kakanj on that day, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, that is the afternoon after the Ovnak operation, the afternoon following the night that you stayed in Pojske. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes. After we spent the night at Pojske, on the following day in the afternoon we received orders to go to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get to Kakanj and when did you arrive there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: We were driven by buses again. We went to a village called Sabac and we got there at night. I really can't remember the exact time, but I do know it was at night. And we stayed the night there at a village called Sabac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the operation in Kakanj then commence?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Well, we got to that village called Sabac near Kakanj that night; we spent the night there. And on the next day -- well, we spent the next day in that village. And the next night we went into action, so that in the early morning of the following day we started the operation at Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to ask you any questions about that operation, but if we could go back to the operation in Ovnak that morning that you described to the Trial Chamber. You said that you were engaging the HVO forces. Could you please assist us with the number of people in your company who were involved in that operation.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I really don't know the exact number of soldiers in that company, but I suppose there were about 80 of us. In my own squad, I think there were from seven to eight soldiers, no more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were engaged in this operation, did you at any time enter any houses or buildings or see anybody else enter premises like that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: In the course of that operation, we came upon some houses and we went into those houses. Following the orders from the squad commander, we went in to make sure there was no one in there, that there were no soldiers there. We went in and we checked whether there were any soldiers there or not. After establishing that there were soldiers [as interpreted] in those houses, we would leave and that was it. And in the same way, my colleagues from my squad went into some houses, but not all. There were some smaller houses where we could see through the windows that there was nobody in there. We did not even go in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I clarify for the transcript. Did you find any soldiers in any of these houses or buildings?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: No, we did not. We did not find any soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you go into the houses?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: The squad commander simply did not want us to not check out those houses because he felt that there was a possibility for soldiers hiding in those houses and that we might have been threatened and that we could have been attacked from behind. And we had to check whether there was anyone in those houses or not, and then we went ahead with our operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in those houses, did you take any goods or see anybody in your units take any goods from those houses?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Definitely not. None of the soldiers in my squad or in my platoon took anything; I did not see that. There were cases of soldiers in the course of such operations when they entered houses, taking a bottle of water or fruit juice or a piece of bread, and that was all. But no one definitely took any goods from those houses, because at that moment we were engaged in a military operation, that's the way we saw it. And what we wanted was to stay alive. And I myself -- my colleagues, I mean it didn't even cross our minds to go and take something like that and risk our lives. And that would have slowed us down and that might have cost our lives basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an ordinary soldier, could you inform the Trial Chamber what orders and instructions, if any, you got from your command before you went into this operation about how to deal with houses, residences, and buildings.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the occasion of every operation during my time within the 7th Brigade, on the occasion of every operation either the commander or someone from the command would address us and issue such orders, that is to say, do not kill innocent people, do not kill women and children, do not kill prisoners, and do not destroy any property. Those were the orders and the instructions that we would get prior to every single operation during my time at the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that morning in the Ovnak area, did you witness any destruction of houses or buildings by the units of your brigade, by the people you were with?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: The only damage that I saw was bullet holes, bullets that had ricocheted or something like that, but there was no other damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about bullet holes. What had happened to the HVO that you were fighting against that morning?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: After they stopped resisting our forces and started to withdraw, we followed them. We were chasing them, so to say. We were engaged in that chase up until the moment when we received orders to stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those orders were received around noon on the day you told us. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: That's right. Early at noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this operation, did you see any other members of any other brigades and units of the Bosnian army present and involved in this operation?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of that operation, I did see members of other brigades who were in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any civilians in the area?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Not in the course of the operation. After completing the operation -- well, there were quite a few civilians there in all those areas which had been liberated during the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And any members of civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were the representatives of the civil defence. And as far as I know, they should have taken over the control over those areas that we had crossed, the villages that had been liberated in that area, the area that we had covered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omic, you have talked about receiving a number of orders during that day. Could you assist the Trial Chamber with the way in which communications worked within your squad and higher up through the chain of command as well.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the means of communication?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. How were orders conveyed, how did communication take place from the command down to you and back again, please.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: We as soldiers communicated with the squad commander, and he communicated with us on the basis of hand signals and his voice. And he communicated with the platoon commander in the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how the platoon commander was communicating with those above him?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I think that he had the radio device, the platoon commander. I think he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omic, I'm not going to ask you any more questions about operations following Ovnak, but could you inform us whether in the summer of 1993 you were promoted?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the summer of 1993 - I think it was in July - I was promoted and I became squad commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of November 1993, where were you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of November 1993, I was sent by the command of the 7th Muslim Brigade to Sarajevo for training. This was the training for commanders of reconnaissance units, and it was organised by the General Staff in Sarajevo at the barracks that used to be called Marsalka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you participate in that training for?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: That training lasted two months exactly, November and December 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not involved in the military operations in the Vares area, were you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: No. Because at that time I was on training in Sarajevo, at that time that I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already said to the Trial Chamber that you have served in the Bosnian army since then and that you were appointed as a major. When was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I was promoted to the rank of major after the war, in 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are currently with the UN. How long will you be on mission in Congo for?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: One year. But I started in November last year and it will run until November this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Omic. I have no questions for you, but my learned friends from the Prosecution may have some additional questions. Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any questions for Mr. Omic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution for their cross-examination. Cross-examined by Mr. Neuner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Omic. My name is Matthias Neuner, and I am appearing here on behalf of the Prosecution and I am going to put a couple of questions to you. If you don't understand any of these questions, please ask me to repeat the question and I'm also prepared to rephrase the question. Mr. Omic, who -- what is the name of your immediate commander in the SUP unit of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in 1993? Can you please state the name?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: My squad commander at the time was Kasim Kokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your squad commander reported to the 1st Company commander I understood. Can you please state his name, 1st Company commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in 1993.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: The squad commander didn't have to report to the company commander; he had to report to the platoon commander, whose name was Sukrija Durmis, whereas the platoon commander had to report to the company commander, whose name was Ragib Catic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Ragib Catic, he reported to the battalion commander. And in May/June 1993 during the operation in Ovnak, the commander of the 2nd Battalion was Mr. Serif Patkovic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about Mr. Serif Patkovic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: At that time I knew nothing about him apart from the fact that he was an officer from the former JNA. And I knew that at that time he was the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether Mr. Patkovic was promoted during the time period you stayed within the 2nd Battalion in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I don't think he was. I'm not sure, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that your barracks were located in the secondary school in Bilmiste in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That is the same school that I had completed just a few months earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other units' commanders stationed at this secondary school in Bilmiste in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of unit commanders from the 7th Brigade? If that's the case, my answer is yes. But there were commanders from other units from that battalion who were in that building. Because the 2nd Battalion was also in that building, in that school. The commanders of other units from the 2nd Battalion were also in that school, in that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be a fair summary that the command of the 2nd Battalion stayed in the secondary school in Bilmiste, as did the brigade command of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your 2nd Battalion command, were they -- was this command staying on the same floor as the brigade command or on different floors?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: No. In Bilmiste there were two buildings, or rather two schools. We, the 2nd Battalion, were in one of the buildings with the battalion command and all the units, and in adjacent building, that's where the brigade command was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "adjacent building." How far away from the building where the 2nd Battalion was housed, how far away was this adjacent building where the commands of the brigade stayed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: From the building that the 2nd Battalion was in to the building that the brigade command was in, it's about 30 metres. They are linked via a corridor. It was possible to leave the battalion command and enter the building in which the brigade command was located. So it was about 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you yourself, did you ever enter the premises where the brigade command stayed in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I entered that building, not the offices, but I did go to the building in which the brigade command was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do in that building?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I cleaned it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The offices of the commander, where were they -- of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, where were the offices located when you cleaned the building?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: They were probably in their offices performing their daily duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the office itself, where was the office located of the brigade commander? On the ground floor? On the first floor?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: The brigade commander's office was on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know about any staff officers' meeting taking place -- how frequently, for example, was your superior meeting with senior officers?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Well, as a soldier I had no information about such matters. I didn't know how frequently there were staff meetings. As soldiers we had meetings with the squad commander, but I really don't know how frequently my superior officers would meet the brigade commander or members of the brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question relating to the secondary school: Was there a kind of logistical section on the compound of the school where -- a warehouse where equipment and materiel could be stored?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a quartermaster equipment warehouse in the basement of that very same building. I'm not quite sure how to explain this, but if you enter via the door where is to the side, right next to that door there was the entrance to the warehouse for quartermaster equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, you're referring to the building of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, or are you referring to the building where the command of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was located? Where was the warehouse exactly?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I thought that you were asking me about the building in which the brigade command was located, so I was thinking of the building in which the brigade command was located. In the basement of that building, there was a warehouse which contained quartermaster equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified you joined the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in March 1993. Did you receive any training upon joining the unit or thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: We had training in the unit on a daily basis, whenever we weren't involved in an operation or whenever there weren't any other daily tasks that we had to carry out. There was training at all times on such occasions in the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive also any specific training relating to war booty and what procedures to be followed? Did you get any advice on war booty during these trainings?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: As part of the training that we were provided with, tactical training and other sorts of training, we were also provided with instructions as to how to conduct ourselves in combat and as to how to use weapons and ammunition -- what to do with weapons and ammunition when we captured weapons and ammunition that belonged to the enemy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to the wider area of Ovnak in the beginning of June 1993, and was this first of all an operation which was under the command of a tactical group?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, I was a member of the 1st Squad. As a soldier, I really didn't know which formation the battalion brigad [as interpreted] was in. I didn't know whether some sort of a tactical group had been formed because no one provided me with such information of that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. type. So I really don't know whether we were in fact part of some sort of a tactical group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned several times the place or the location of Pojske. I have here a map with me. Would you be in a position to show where that place, Pojske, was to which you went at the beginning of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, can I have these copies distributed, please. This is a combined version of Defence exhibits DH87 until DH90, a map from the west -- the area west of Zenica, for the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please point to the place or location Pojske -- which is called Pojske.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: It doesn't say that this is Pojske, but Pojske is beneath the village of Vrselje; it's in this area here, but you can't see the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please encircle the area which you referred to as Pojske and mark it with a 1 next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next day when the combat operations started, can you please mark with an arrow in which direction your unit went, to which villages did you go and where was the retreating point, so to speak? Can you please first of all point with a pointer to the direction in which you went and later mark it -- or mark it with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: The area that we went to to carry out our operation was called Crni Vrh, but I really couldn't show you the direction of our advance. As I have already said, I was an ordinary soldier at the time. I didn't have a map and no one had issued orders to me on a map and I never saw what the advance axis was for our unit on the map. As a private, I'd been assigned the task in the field. Commanders of the squad would point to individual hills, individual areas, individual points, but I never had a map, never received a map from my superior officer. So I wouldn't want to make a mistake by indicating the route that my unit took to advance on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just -- did the hamlets, villages, places through which you went through during your operation, did they have any signs, like name signs? Did you see any village names while you were advancing?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time. During that operation, I knew that I was in the Ovnak sector, but I didn't pass through any large villages. But the houses that we came across in the course of our operation didn't have any -- any signs indicating the name of the place. There were no such signs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many kilometres did you proceed during the operation? You were walking for hours? You were walking for minutes? How far, from your recollection, would you think you would have marched that day? You said you started early in the morning and at noon you rested.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I said that we set off around midnight before the operation, the night before the operation, and then we walked until dawn. And at dawn, we commenced the operation and we finished around lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what point -- or before you returned to Pojske, did you meet any other unit so -- and maybe from that point you have returned. Did you encounter -- I mean ABiH unit so that you knew the areas occupied by ABiH forces so that this is a convenient point to return? I'm just asking did you -- do you recall any units which you might have met along your way from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: While the operation was ongoing, I didn't see members of other brigades, of other units, apart from units from the 7th Muslim Brigade. Once the operation was over, I then saw men who were not from our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this is a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have our break now. It's 25 to 4.00 and we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to Mr. Neuner to continue with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omic, having had the break, a couple of minutes to think, do you maybe now recall in which direction your march or your operation went on this particular day, 7th or 8th of June, 1993, in the Ovnak area?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already said, we were moving from the village of Pojske towards the village of Crni Vrh. I really can't indicate the route on the map. I am afraid of making a mistake -- because let me repeat, that I did not receive an order on a map, and I didn't see a plan for the operation on a map -- with reference to a map at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Just one more question. If I look on the map which you have encircled, where you have a specific location encircled, Pojske, there is a hamlet or village there which is called Vrselje. Do you see that, Vrselje, village which is more or less around the circle which you draw. Do you see that on your map?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you yourself been in Vrselje either before you came or before you went away from the area?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I went to the village of Vrselje after the war. I don't know in which year exactly, but I do know that I went there after the war. If you want to reach the village of Vrselje, you have to pass through the village of Pojske, although you can't see it on the map. If you look at the map you will see elevation 950 I think. Just before the elevation there is the village of Vrselje, and the village of Pojske is before the village of Vrselje. I'm not sure, but I think that the village of Vrselje has been marked twice. I think that this is the village of Pojske, whereas Vrselje is almost on the top of this hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that for the -- I will call it now for today for the so-called Ovnak operation, for the operation in the Ovnak area, that the -- or that a command post was located in the village of Vrselje on 6th, 7th, and 8th June. Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I know that now. However, at the time that the operation was being carried out, I didn't know that the command post was in the village of Vrselje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned after the operation to Pojske, can you please clarify, did you take then a bus to Kakanj or did you walk? You might have said it already, but can you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Having returned from the Ovnak operation, having returned to the village of Pojske, we spent the night there. We had a good breakfast. We had a rest, and then in the afternoon buses took us to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while leaving the more or less immediate combat area, were you checked or your bus in which you were sitting, was this bus stopped and checked by anybody?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: What do you mean checked? We were stopped at the checkpoint in Vlasi. There was a checkpoint there, but what do you mean checked? I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Checked in the sense of that on the road towards Zenica probably, on the road that there was -- that there were some uniformed persons who maybe asked some questions to the soldiers, like you, who have boarded the bus. Did this occur? If it didn't occur, just state so.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: After we boarded the buses, we weren't checked, as I have said. But before getting on the buses, the commander of the unit, or rather my squad commander checked the squad, and before, the military police was present, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on your way to Kakanj did you stop at Zenica, at the Bilmiste barracks, or did you drive through with the bus right away?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I know that we went to Kakanj on that very same day. As to whether we went to the barracks in Zenica or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as additional questions are concerned, the Judges deliberated a while ago. In theory, if Defence counsel is acting independently, they should not be taking the floor. So only Brigadier Kubura's Defence counsel has the right to additional questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have no additional questions arising from Mr. Neuner's questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a few brief questions of a technical and military kind. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 31, line 14, you said that the military police were there, as far as you can remember. Since all this happened a very long time ago, and perhaps you don't remember everything, but when you were in Ovnak were there any elements of the military police there or not?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Military police members were in Ovnak, too, and they were monitoring the movement of units from Ovnak towards Pojske after the operation had been completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that they were monitoring, what does that mean exactly? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether these are the orders that they received, but given the way they were behaving at that point in time I think that they were observing whether soldiers were carrying weapons that weren't theirs at that point in time and observing whether they were carrying property that they had found in the village. I think that that is what their task was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you returned to Ovnak - this is something you haven't mentioned, you said nothing about it and I didn't understand this part of your testimony very clearly - at that time was there fighting with the HVO? Were you exchanging fire? Did you return to Ovnak, and was the place deserted? There were no HVO soldiers there. When you arrived there, was there ongoing fighting or not? What could you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: In the early morning hours when we started to carry out the operation, the HVO mounted a fierce resistance; however, it did not last for very long, not even an hour. After that, they started withdrawing, and we continued to carry out our operation by pursuing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When they withdrew, there were no more HVO soldiers in Ovnak when you entered the place?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I didn't see a single one after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you did not take any HVO prisoners in Ovnak?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: No, not in that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you can remember, were there any civilians and inhabitants of Ovnak who had remained there, because you said that you had entered the houses. Did you meet any civilians there or had the village been completely deserted?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: While carrying out the operation, as I have already said, we passed by some houses. We didn't find any civilians or military members in those houses. I heard that in one place the civilians had taken refuge. They had all assembled in one place. That's what I had been told, though I didn't personal witness that. I heard they had taken refuge in a safe place while the operation was being carried out. But while we were passing by those houses in the course of the operation, we did not come across any soldiers or any civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Kakanj, my question is the same: When you arrived there, there was no ongoing fighting or was there fighting there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: We started the operation, as I said, in the early morning hours, and the fighting in Kakanj was fierce. However, in the places that we passed through we did not meet any soldiers or civilians. We reached a place where the -- inhabited by Bosniaks and Muslims. It had been encircled for two or three days by HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you can remember, in Kakanj the soldiers who were involved in the operation, did they take any prisoners there or not?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't. I really don't have any information about the other units. But as for the unit that I was in, we did not take anyone prisoner in the course of that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that you were in the 1st Squad of the 1st Platoon of the 1st Company of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Brigade. It's complicated, but it's necessary to go right up that chain. You were at the very bottom because you weren't even a squad commander, although you're a major right now. But at that time you were a private and so the squad was commanded by Kasim Kokic. As far as you know, within the 2nd Battalion, which was furthest removed from you, were there any foreigners or were you all from that country or from that area? Were there any non-Bosniak combatants there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: In my battalion, all the soldiers were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not only from the area of Zenica since Zenica was a town in which a lot of refugees from other areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina had arrived. And as a result, there were people from the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But they were all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There weren't any foreigners of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My very last question of a technical nature. When you were in the 7th Brigade, did you receive a salary or did you never receive any sort of salary?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: In the course of the war, we received some form of compensation, and they didn't call it a salary. We were given some Bosnian dinars. That's what they called them at the time. Each soldier was supposed to receive a certain amount. However, this wasn't paid to the soldiers on a regular basis and it wasn't a very significant amount. I don't think you could even have bought a toothbrush and toothpaste or shaving utensils. At that time, these items were very expensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution. Further cross-examination by Mr. Neuner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omic, just a question. You were asked by the Presiding Judge about the military police being present in the area. Do you know whether this military police was from the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, or was it from another unit?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, at that time there was a military police squad in the 2nd Battalion and there was military police at the brigade level as well. I believe that both formations, the military police units in the battalion and in the brigade, I think they were both there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they were both there, what do you mean by "there"? In what location or -- in Ovnak or somewhere else? I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: When I say that they were both there or present, what I mean to say is that the formations of military police from within the 2nd Battalion and the military police formations which were within the brigade, not all members of the military police but there were members of military police from both of these forces, and they were stationed at the exit from Ovnak when we went from Ovnak to Pojske.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say when you went from Ovnak to Pojske, was this when you came? Was this when you returned? Please just clarify. When you returned from the area or when you went to the wider area of Ovnak/Pojske?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: No, not before the start of the operation. When we were coming back after completing the operation in those early evening hours, they were present along that route that we took from Ovnak to Pojske.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did these military policemen tell you what they were doing or why they were checking people? Did they mention something to you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: No, they did not explain the nature of their job. They were just standing there. I can't really say that it was a checkpoint; it wasn't a traditional sort of checkpoint. They just -- they were just standing there at one point, and they were supervising the movement of their units. And they would check out individual soldiers in order to check what they had in their rucksacks. And that's how I concluded that that must have been their task, although they did not tell us what was the nature of their job at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you yourself were asked for your ID or you had to open your bag, you yourself? I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: No, they did not ask me to. But they did it at random. And at that time we had kind of a booklet of the Army of the BH, and they were not normally checking our IDs or anything. But we used to wear ribbons of different colour so we could recognise each other in the course of battle and also outside of battle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were interested which units or which soldiers belonged to which unit were moving in which direction --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just said "we had ribbons in the course of the operations." Could you describe that armbands that you were wearing? And then I'll give you the floor later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just a piece of cloth in a given colour. For every operation we had that in order to be able to recognise one another in the forest or when there was poor visibility we had certain colours, for example, white or green. It was a simple piece of cloth in a given colour, which was either on our left or right shoulder, depending on the orders we were given, in order to be able to recognise one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just coming back to my question. The military police soldier -- first of all, how many military policemen were standing there? One person? Two persons? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't tell you the exact number, but I don't think I'll go wrong if I say it was perhaps one squad between six and ten people, more or less, but I can't give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And judging from what happened -- you yourself approached this checkpoint or these four or five to six people with how many soldiers? You were not alone or you were alone?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: We moved as a company, the 1st Company, in a column. And then the other units were following us. And we all took the same route, from Ovnak to Pojske, so that all my colleagues or the colleagues from my own unit and from the other units had to go past that place. I can't really call it a checkpoint. It wasn't a checkpoint proper; it was just a place where they were standing and overseeing the movement of units from Ovnak to Pojske.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned that other units were involved, too, and were going through that checkpoint. Which other units are you referring to which were coming right behind after your squad?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: What I mean is the units from the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade, the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd Company, and the other units. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All three units from the 2nd Battalion were passing with you towards Pojske when you returned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Look, I was within the 1st Company of the 1st Battalion of the 1st Squad. So I was at the front of the 1st Company and -- as we were going from Ovnak to Pojske. I myself did not actually see all the other units. I did not see whether they actually did go past that place where the military police were. I did not see it, but I believe they did because we were moving along that route. And since we all took the same route, I suppose everybody must have gone past that place where the military police was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that you were all moving past that place. Where did you initially meet? Was this kilometres before or just shortly before this if I call it temporary checkpoint. You just met the other units shortly there before, can you just clarify, or you were walking already for kilometres with the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Company of the 2nd Battalion in a row?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Look, after the operation was completed, the company with the platoons and squads were stationed in one place, and the same went for the other company and all the other units. So the squad commanders checked squads, and the platoon commanders checked platoons, whether anyone was missing, whether anyone had been wounded, the regular sort of military check. And when we were given orders to go back to Pojske, we moved towards Pojske in a column. And so one company was initially in one direction, the other in another, et cetera. And when we were told to stop from those initial positions, we went back along that route and we went Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. past the place where the military police was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So basically all companies from the 2nd Battalion moved past that checkpoint towards Pojske on the 7th or the 8th, you don't recall exactly, of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat this. I did not stay at that checkpoint and I did not actually see with my own eyes all these units passing by. But since we're all going the same way, I believe they must have done. I myself did not actually physically see them all, but I believe they must have done since we were all going the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question for clarification. The bus you boarded then, I think it was the next day, after your breakfast - you mentioned that - on this bus was there only your squad or were there also members from the other companies of the 2nd Battalion? Who was boarding that bus, please?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: The orders were very clear in that respect. The 1st Company was to board a bus. When we -- when the bus was full, the rest of the company boarded the next bus. So in one bus there were mostly members of one and the same unit, but if there was only one left behind, I mean anyone who could not board the first bus, they would have boarded the bus with members of some other company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses all together are we talking here?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your bus went towards Kakanj. Can you just clarify, towards Zagrada near Kakanj -- I didn't get the name of the location near Kakanj or at Kakanj where you went. Can you please spell the name of that location where you went to.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: When we got to that village I asked the locals what the name of the village was and they said it was Zagrada.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you spell it, please?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's Z-a-g-r-a-d-a.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this a village which is a few kilometres away from Kakanj proper?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I rise hesitantly, but in our submission this is outside of the scope of the questions hat Your Honours asked and could have been asked at the time after examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm prepared to withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just have one question left with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The buses or the bus -- you went to Zagrada. Did the other buses also go to Zagrada - it's my last question - or did they go to somewhere else with the other company members?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Yes. All buses who were driving members of the 2nd Battalion got to Zagrada there, and I remember it was a fairly inaccessible village, and the buses had a great deal of trouble in turning around. That's how I know that there were more buses and that all members of the 2nd Battalion got to Zagrada by bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to summarise, more or less the soldiers which went through the checkpoint towards Pojske the next day boarded a bus and went towards Kakanj, to be precise, the village of Zagrada?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, only one question. Further examination by Mr. Dixon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you mention the operation in Ovnak being completed in the morning and you then withdrew to the village of Pojske with the other members of the 2nd Battalion, did any of you go back to the Ovnak area that day or there after?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN OMIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. After the operation, we came to the village of Pojske. We were tired and we spent the night there. And on the next day we went to Kakanj. And if anyone had wanted to go back, there was simply no possibility for anyone to go back and catch another bus and then get to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, your hearing has been completed. I would like to thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber for having travelled such a long way to testify. You have made your contribution to the establishment of the truth and you have answered all the questions that we wanted to ask you. However, before we release you, I'd like to know whether the Defence -- no, rather the Prosecution would like to tender this map. Now, what you need to do is write your name and the date of today on the map, and then you must sign the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: While this is being done, Your Honour, I just had a little conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- with the Defence about this map. My understanding is there are no objections by both Defence counsels against this map, but I was just told to state for the record that this map is not coming out of DH87 till DH90; it is 1:50.000, 1:50.000 measurement, and it is accepted, that is my understanding, by both parties that this is an adequate map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right then. The Defence, you do not object to this map being tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objections, but for the sake of the transcript we would just like to stress once again that it is a kind of compilation of maps, as it were, because this map shows things clearly because you can -- I mean, you can see certain places indicated twice, such as Susanj, Vrselje, et cetera, but we have nothing against it being tendered because the witness found the place where he was, and that's why the Prosecution is supposedly suggesting this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right then. Your point will be included in the transcript. Registrar, could you give us a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. So it is tendered as Prosecution document P959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, please, for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to be complete, this piece of the evidence is admitted into the record under the reference P959. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a good idea to ask you to repeat because the initial indication was P595. Major, as I was saying I would like to thank you very much indeed, and on behalf of the Judges I would like to wish you all the best on your return trip and in the course of your duties. I am now going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm going to take this opportunity and ask the usher to bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Originally you had planned on two and a half hours for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But after the proofing we realised that perhaps half the time and perhaps even less would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
